sections.title: باب 1 — متن (19)

paras.text: … participation, continued alongside. In the authoritarian period the executive mostly remained non-political. Powers remained in the hands of martial-law administrators or ruling military generals. In this system the members of the executive remained powerless, because in these systems powers were severely centralised. The executive mostly consisted of the members of the Convention Party (the ruler’s party), or of the bureaucracy, big traders, jagirdars and industrialists etc. In this system the attitude of the executive always remained authoritarian. The authoritarian administration remained answerable to one individual and worked as the personal employees of that ruler. In this kind of executive there was no collective or public answerability. In some authoritarian periods the ruler’s supporting politicians were brought together to form a political party, and the custom of civil and military rule was established.

paras.text: In the democratic periods the elected legislature makes laws for the country. In the first democratic period (1947–1958), the members of the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan who had been elected in the elections held before independence, in the British Indian Parliament, and who were representatives of the areas of Pakistan; later a central legislature was elected through the provincial assemblies. In the democratic period the representatives were truly elected representatives of the people. The legislature worked for constitution-making and democratic law-making. Despite many weaknesses, the legislature of that period worked in a democratic manner and enjoyed public confidence and support. In the democratic period (1971–1977), as a result of Pakistan’s first general elections, an elected legislature came into being, which, by the consensus of public wishes and political parties, approved the Constitution of 1973. In the third period (1988–1999) the elected political democratic legislature kept working. Public opinion was respected, and despite some defects the legislature adopted a democratic style. The legislature ended all the undemocratic amendments of the authoritarian period and restored the constitution to its original form.

paras.text: In the authoritarian periods the legislature remained a puppet. Ayub Khan’s legislature was elected through Basic Democracies, in which the Convention Muslim League, the party supporting Ayub Khan, had a majority. Its members had no power except to say yes in yes to the dictator. Other parties’ representation was as good as non-existent. In this way, on the one hand it was undemocratic, and secondly, the legislature of Ayub Khan was nothing more than a machine for giving legal and constitutional shape to its authoritarian wishes and measures. In General Zia-ul-Haq’s first and second periods, a nominated Majlis-e-Shura was formed; non-party elections were held and Muhammad Khan Junejo was appointed Prime Minister. This legislature was nothing except a rubber stamp, through which General Zia provided legal protection to his illegal and unconstitutional measures. It was a non-political, non-party legislature consisting of Zia’s supporters, which did not enjoy public support, and this legislature, by the Eighth Amendment, spoiled the shape of the constitution, through which very important powers …

… participation, continued alongside. In the authoritarian period the executive mostly remained non-political. Powers remained in the hands of martial-law administrators or ruling military generals. In this system the members of the executive remained powerless, because in these systems powers were severely centralised. The executive mostly consisted of the members of the Convention Party (the ruler’s party), or of the bureaucracy, big traders, jagirdars and industrialists etc. In this system the attitude of the executive always remained authoritarian. The authoritarian administration remained answerable to one individual and worked as the personal employees of that ruler. In this kind of executive there was no collective or public answerability. In some authoritarian periods the ruler’s supporting politicians were brought together to form a political party, and the custom of civil and military rule was established.

In the democratic periods the elected legislature makes laws for the country. In the first democratic period (1947–1958), the members of the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan who had been elected in the elections held before independence, in the British Indian Parliament, and who were representatives of the areas of Pakistan; later a central legislature was elected through the provincial assemblies. In the democratic period the representatives were truly elected representatives of the people. The legislature worked for constitution-making and democratic law-making. Despite many weaknesses, the legislature of that period worked in a democratic manner and enjoyed public confidence and support. In the democratic period (1971–1977), as a result of Pakistan’s first general elections, an elected legislature came into being, which, by the consensus of public wishes and political parties, approved the Constitution of 1973. In the third period (1988–1999) the elected political democratic legislature kept working. Public opinion was respected, and despite some defects the legislature adopted a democratic style. The legislature ended all the undemocratic amendments of the authoritarian period and restored the constitution to its original form.

In the authoritarian periods the legislature remained a puppet. Ayub Khan’s legislature was elected through Basic Democracies, in which the Convention Muslim League, the party supporting Ayub Khan, had a majority. Its members had no power except to say yes in yes to the dictator. Other parties’ representation was as good as non-existent. In this way, on the one hand it was undemocratic, and secondly, the legislature of Ayub Khan was nothing more than a machine for giving legal and constitutional shape to its authoritarian wishes and measures. In General Zia-ul-Haq’s first and second periods, a nominated Majlis-e-Shura was formed; non-party elections were held and Muhammad Khan Junejo was appointed Prime Minister. This legislature was nothing except a rubber stamp, through which General Zia provided legal protection to his illegal and unconstitutional measures. Comparison of the powers of the President and the Prime Minister under the Constitution of 1973

In the Constitution of 1973, after the Eighteenth Constitutional Amendment, a balance has been created in the powers of the President and the Prime Minister. According to the constitution the President is the symbolic and constitutional head of the country, whereas the Prime Minister is the head of government and the administrative head of the country. The responsibility for all administrative affairs rests on the Prime Minister and his cabinet. The formal power of appointing ministers and giving them departments belongs to the President, but in fact the Prime Minister presents the names of ministers and the departments to the President, and the President is bound to accept them. The Prime Minister can advise the removal of any minister and presides over the meetings of the cabinet. The Prime Minister is bound to keep the President informed of government activities. It can be said in this way that the real administrative powers of the country belong to the Prime Minister.

The Prime Minister, besides being a member of the legislature, is also the Leader of the House. He is also the leader of the majority party in the National Assembly. He takes part in the sessions of the legislature. Ministers prepare all legal proposals (bills or drafts) in consultation with the Prime Minister, and in this connection the Prime Minister’s directions have importance. The President summons the session of any house. At the beginning of the parliamentary year the President addresses a joint session. In case of disagreement, the legislature can approve the same law again. According to the constitution the most important power of the Prime Minister with regard to the legislature is that he can dissolve the National Assembly. Under the constitution the President signs the financial laws of the National Assembly. After the approval of the budget it is sent to the President for signature. The President of Pakistan appoints the Auditor General of Pakistan for the audit of finances in the country and appoints the members of the National Economic Council and the National Finance Council. The financial drafts are presented in the National Assembly by the Finance Minister. The annual budget of the country is prepared and presented according to the directions of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister in practice controls the national treasury. Regarding the national treasury, after the National Assembly it is the Prime Minister who is empowered, rather the real powers belong to the Prime Minister, because the Prime Minister’s party has a majority in the National Assembly and the budget presented by the government is approved. Hence the Prime Minister also has superiority in financial affairs.

دستور 1973ء کے تحت صدر اور وزیرِ اعظم کے اختیارات کا موازنہ

آئین 1973ء میں اٹھارویں آئینی ترمیم کے بعد صدر اور وزیرِ اعظم کے اختیارات میں توازن پیدا کیا گیا ہے۔ دستور کے مطابق صدر ملک کا علامتی اور آئینی سربراہ ہے۔ جبکہ وزیرِ اعظم سربراہِ حکومت اور ملک کا انتظامی سربراہ ہے۔ تمام انتظامی اُمور کی ذمہ داری وزیرِ اعظم اور اُس کی کابینہ پر ہے۔ وزراء کی تقرری اور اُن کو محکمے دینے کا رسمی اختیار صدر کو حاصل ہے لیکن وزراء کے نام اور محکمے دراصل وزیرِ اعظم ہی صدر کو پیش کرتا ہے اور صدر اُسے ماننے کا پابند ہے۔ وزیرِ اعظم کسی بھی وزیر کو برطرف کرنے کا مشورہ دے سکتا ہے اور کابینہ کے اجلاسوں کی صدارت کرتا ہے۔ وزیرِ اعظم صدر کو حکومتی سرگرمیوں سے باخبر رکھنے کا پابند ہے۔ اِس طرح یہ کہا جا سکتا ہے کہ ملک کے حقیقی انتظامی اختیارات وزیرِ اعظم کو حاصل ہیں۔

وزیرِ اعظم مقننہ کا رکن ہونے کے علاوہ قائدِ ایوان بھی ہوتا ہے۔ وہ قومی اسمبلی میں اکثریتی جماعت کا قائد بھی ہوتا ہے۔ وہ مقننہ کے اجلاسوں میں شرکت کرتا ہے۔ تمام قانونی تجاویز (بل یا مسودے) وزراء وزیرِ اعظم کی مشاورت سے تیار کرتے ہیں اور اُس سلسلے میں وزیرِ اعظم کی ہدایات کو اہمیت حاصل ہوتی ہے۔ صدر کسی بھی ایوان کا اجلاس طلب کرتا ہے، ہر پارلیمانی سال کے آغاز پر صدر مشترکہ اجلاس سے خطاب کرتا ہے۔ اِختلاف کی صورت میں مقننہ اُس قانون کو دوبارہ بھی منظور کر سکتی ہے۔ مقننہ کے حوالے سے وزیرِ اعظم کا سب سے اہم اختیار یہ ہے کہ وہ قومی اسمبلی کو توڑ سکتا ہے۔ آئین کی رو سے صدر قومی اسمبلی کے مالیاتی قوانین پر دستخط کرتا ہے۔ بجٹ کی منظوری کے بعد اسے صدر کے دستخط کیلئے بھیجا جاتا ہے۔ صدرِ پاکستان ملک میں مالیات کی پڑتال کیلئے آڈیٹر جنرل آف پاکستان کی تقرری اور قومی اِقتصادی کونسل و قومی مالیاتی کونسل کے ارکان کا تقرر کرتا ہے۔ مالیاتی مسودات وزیرِ خزانہ ہی قومی اسمبلی میں پیش کرتا ہے۔ ملک کا سالانہ بجٹ وزیرِ اعظم کی ہدایات کے مطابق تیار اور پیش کیا جاتا ہے۔ وزیرِ اعظم عملی طور پر قومی خزانے کو کنٹرول کرتا ہے۔ قومی خزانے کے بارے میں قومی اسمبلی کے بعد وزیرِ اعظم ہی بااختیار ہے بلکہ اصل اختیارات وزیرِ اعظم کو حاصل ہیں۔ کیونکہ وزیرِ اعظم کی پارٹی کی قومی اسمبلی میں اکثریت ہوتی ہے اور حکومت کی طرف سے پیش کردہ بجٹ کو منظور کیا جاتا ہے۔ لہٰذا وزیرِ اعظم کو مالیاتی اُمور میں بھی فوقیت حاصل ہے۔
